full_judgment:
2. Respondent No.1 as pre-emptor filed three cases for pre-emption under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949. The pre-emption cases were filed in respect of three kabalas on the assertion that the pre-emptor is a co-sharer of the land. 

 5. On appeal the lower appellate Court reversed the judgment of the trial Court and allowed the pre-emption cases on the ground that the pre-emptor was a co-sharer in the land as the partition decree was not executed in full and that the tenancy of the pre-emptor and the vendors were still ejmali and that there was no evidence that the ejmali property was separated. A learned Single Judge of the High Court Division affirmed the judgment of the lower appellate Court. 

 8. Leave was granted in the review petition to consider the submission of Mr Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned Advocate appearing for the pre-emptee-appellant, to consider whether in view of the provisions of section 2(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure read with section 24(11) of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949, the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division erred in law in affirming the decision of the court of appeal below which was based on the reasoning’s that the final decree of partition passed in Title Suit No. 36 of 1975 had not been fully executed and whether this material aspect of this case has not been considered by this Division in disposing of the petition for leave to appeal. 

 9. Leave was further granted to consider the question of law as to the effect of a final decree in a partition suit on the co-sharership of the pre-emptor in a pre-emption proceeding under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949. 

 10. The pre-emptor Abdul Karim and his father Momin Biswas purchased five kathas i.e. 0.0825 Ajutangsha of land from CS Plot No. 968 in equal share by registered deed on 24-4-60 and thereafter on the death of his father the pre-emptor filed partition suit against the other heirs of his father in the court of Sub-Judge, 1st Court, Faridpur being TS No. 36 of 1975 and the said suit was decreed in preliminary form on 30-11-77 and thereafter an Advocate Commissioner was appointed for distributing and separating the boundary of the saham of the ejmali land to the parties of the said partition suit and the Advocate Commissioner. accordingly distributed and separated the saham and filed his statement on 2-10-78. Thereafter, the final decree was passed on 23-12-78 and the suit property fell in the saham of respondent Nos. 2, 3 and 4 and they possessed the property in their respective share in khas. Respondent Nos. 2-4 sold the suit property on 29-12-84 to the Appellant long after the final decree was passed in Title. Suit No. 36 of 1975 and thereafter the pre-emptor respondent No. 1 filed the pre-emption Miscellaneous Cases on 28-9-85 on the ground of co-sharership. 

 14. A reference to section 2(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure shows that a decree may be either preliminary or final. Explanation to section 2(2) provides that "a decree is preliminary when further proceedings have to be taken before the suit can be completely disposed of. It is final when such adjudication completely disposes of the suit". In a suit for partition, after filing of the report along with the case map, field book, saham list by the Advocate Commissioner final decree takes effect and thereafter remains nothing to be done. In a pre-emption proceeding under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, the question of co-sharership in the tenancy is relevant, but in section 24(1) of Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act the co-sharership in the land is material. In that view of the matter, the passing of the final decree in a partition suit finally determines the rights of the co-sharers in the land. Hence, the application for the pre-emptor-respondents on the basis of co-sharership is not maintainable.
